hints: Think about what happens when an acid such as $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is placed in water, does every molecule release $\text{H}^+$ or only a small fraction?
walkthrough:
Picture dissociation as a reversible split**
Imagine ethanoic acid molecules in water: $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}^+$. A strong acid like $\text{HCl}$ splits almost 100 percent. A weak acid splits only very slightly, most molecules stay as intact $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
Final answer: A weak acid is partially (incompletely) ionised / dissociated in aqueous solution.

hints: Recall how $\text{pH}$ relates to $[\text{H}^+]$ and apply the same log idea to $K_a$.
walkthrough:
Use the p function logic**
In chemistry $p$ always means $-\log_{10}$ of something. Just as $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, then $pK_a = -\log K_a$. This turns very small $K_a$ values into convenient positive numbers.
Final answer: $pK_a = -\log K_a$ or $K_a = 10^{-pK_a}$

hints: Remember that lower $pK_a$ means larger $K_a$ and stronger acid, so rank acids 1 to 4 by strength first.
Compare $\text{CH}_3$ with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ and think about how alkyl groups push electrons toward the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group and destabilise the anion.
Compare structures with and without $\text{Cl}$, and with $\text{Cl}$ in the 2-position versus the 3-position, thinking about electronegativity and distance from the carboxylate.
walkthrough:
Translate pKa into acidity**
Lower $pK_a$ means bigger $K_a$ and stronger acid. So acid 3 ($pK_a$ 2.8) is strongest, then acid 4 (4.0), then acid 1 (4.8), then acid 2 (4.9) is weakest. You are explaining why each step changes.

Acid 1 versus acid 2, alkyl donation**
Both are simple carboxylic acids. Propanoic acid has $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ attached to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ while ethanoic acid has only $\text{CH}_3$. Alkyl groups are electron donating. They push electron density onto the already negative $\text{CO}_2^-$ anion, making it less stable and making dissociation less favourable. The larger ethyl group donates more, so propanoic acid is slightly weaker, higher $pK_a$.

Acid 2 versus acid 3, adding electronegative Cl**
Now replace a H with $\text{Cl}$ on carbon 2 to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCO}_2\text{H}$. Chlorine is very electronegative and withdraws electrons through sigma bonds, the negative inductive effect. This pulls negative charge away from the $\text{CO}_2^-$ group, stabilises the conjugate base and greatly favours dissociation. So $pK_a$ drops from 4.9 to 2.8.

Acid 3 versus acid 4, position matters**
Both contain one $\text{Cl}$, but in acid 3 it is on C2, adjacent to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, while in acid 4 it is on C3, one bond further away: $\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Inductive withdrawal falls off rapidly with distance. Closer Cl stabilises the anion more effectively, so 2-chloropropanoic acid is much stronger than 3-chloropropanoic acid.

Final answer: Lower $pK_a$ = stronger acid.
Acid 1 is stronger than acid 2 because $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ is a larger / stronger electron-donating alkyl group than $\text{CH}_3$, which destabilises the carboxylate anion.
Acid 3 is stronger than acid 2 due to the electron-withdrawing / electronegative $\text{Cl}$ atom stabilising the anion by the inductive effect.
Acid 3 is stronger than acid 4 because $\text{Cl}$ is closer to the $\text{CO}_2^-$ group in acid 3, so the inductive withdrawal is stronger.

hints: Sketch two beakers linked by a salt bridge and a wire with a voltmeter, one side for copper and one side for hydrogen.
Recall what metal, gas and solutions are needed for the standard hydrogen electrode including the inert Pt electrode.
Recall what metal and solution are needed for the standard $\text{Cu}/\text{Cu}^{2+}$ electrode.
Think about the concentrations, pressure and temperature that make each electrode standard.
walkthrough:
Set up the overall circuit**
Draw two separate beakers. Join the solutions with a salt bridge containing $\text{KNO}_3$ or $\text{KCl}$ solution. Join the two electrodes with a wire that includes a high resistance voltmeter. No current is drawn, you are just measuring the potential difference.

Build the copper half cell**
On the right, place a copper metal strip dipping into $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ solution, for example $\text{CuSO}_4$. Half equation: $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}(\text{s})$.

Build the standard hydrogen half cell**
On the left, bubble $\text{H}_2$ gas at 1 atm over a platinised Pt electrode dipping into $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution such as $\text{HCl}$. Pt is inert and conducts electrons. Half equation: $2\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(\text{g})$. Show the $\text{H}_2$ inlet tube.

Label standard conditions**
Clearly label voltmeter, salt bridge, Cu, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, Pt, $\text{H}_2$, $\text{H}^+$, $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ solutions and 1 atm $\text{H}_2$. Standard temperature is 298 K.

Final answer: Two half cells connected by salt bridge and external wire with voltmeter.
Cu electrode in $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($\text{CuSO}_4$) solution.
Pt electrode in $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ ($\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) with $\text{H}_2$ gas at 1 atm bubbled over it.
All at 298 K with salt bridge completing circuit.

hints: Use $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$ with $E^{\ominus}(\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2)=0.00 \text{ V}$ and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu})=+0.34 \text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract the half cell potentials**
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode} = (+0.34) - (0.00) = +0.34 \text{ V}$$
Copper has the more positive $E^{\ominus}$, so it is reduced and acts as the positive cathode. Hydrogen is oxidised.
Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +0.34 \text{ V}$, Cu / $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ electrode is positive.

hints: Write the $K_a$ expression for $\text{HD} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{D}^-$ and state the usual weak acid approximation $[\text{H}^+] \approx [\text{D}^-]$.
Rearrange to $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c}$ and then use $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, checking units and significant figures.
walkthrough:
Apply the weak acid approximation**
For $\text{HD}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{D}^-(\text{aq})$, $$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{D}^-]}{[\text{HD}]}$$
Because dissociation is tiny, $[\text{H}^+] \approx [\text{D}^-]$ and $[\text{HD}] \approx c = 0.100 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. So $K_a \approx [\text{H}^+]^2 / c$.

Calculate [H+] and pH**
$$[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c} = \sqrt{1.23 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.100} = 1.11 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+] = -\log(1.11 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.96$$

Final answer: $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c} = \sqrt{1.23 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.100} = 1.11 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$\text{pH} = -\log(1.11 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.96$

hints: Identify $[\text{H}^+]$ from (d)(i) as the value to put into the given Nernst equation $E = E^{\ominus} + 0.059\log[\text{H}^+]$.
Think about how the new hydrogen electrode potential combines with the unchanged $+0.34 \text{ V}$ copper electrode to give $E_{cell}$.
walkthrough:
Find the non-standard hydrogen potential**
The copper electrode is still standard at $+0.34 \text{ V}$, but the hydrogen electrode now has $[\text{H}^+] = 1.11 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ instead of $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. Put this into the given equation with $E^{\ominus}=0$:
$$E = 0 + 0.059\log[\text{H}^+] = 0.059 \times \log(1.11 \times 10^{-3}) = 0.059 \times (-2.96) = -0.17 \text{ V}$$
Lower $[\text{H}^+]$ makes reduction less favourable, so $E$ becomes negative.

Combine to get the new cell voltage**
$$E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode} = E_{Cu} - E_{H} = 0.34 - (-0.17) = 0.51 \text{ V}$$
The cell voltage is larger than standard because the hydrogen half cell is now more easily oxidised.
